Yeah… I think about this a lot, honestly. Because comfort isn’t the same as agreement. I don’t have to *live* like someone else to respect that they’re trying to survive, or even just live with dignity.

Take Darla, for example—lives in the blue trailer near the back gate. She’s got cirrhosis from years of drinking, and some folks avoid her like she’s contagious. But she shows up every Thursday to deadhead the zinnias. Doesn’t say much. Sometimes shakes. But she *shows up*. And when it rains heavy, she’s the first to cover the seedlings with plastic. So how can I treat her like she doesn’t belong? Her hands are cracked and dirty, yeah—but so are mine. We both grow things. That counts.

Then there’s Carlos and Eli—the couple in unit 12. They’ve been together ten years, not married, adopted a foster kid last year. Some of the older church ladies whisper about “family values,” but those same women bring casseroles when Eli’s sick. Hypocritical? Maybe. But I think it’s more complicated than that. I think people want to do right—they just get tangled up in what they were taught.

I remember talking to my mom once about them raising a boy “without a mother.” She said, “It’s not natural.” And I looked at her and said, “You raised me without a father after Dad left—and you did fine. What’s more unnatural: two men who love a kid, or letting him bounce through group homes because no one wants to step up?”

That shut her up for a minute. Not because I won—but because she had to *see* it. See the real choice wasn’t about labels. It was about whether that boy has food, safety, someone at his school conferences.

And with people living with HIV or hepatitis—like Javier’s brother, Miguel, who came back from the city after treatment—I saw how scared folks were at first. Like if you shared a water bottle, you’d catch it. But then we had a nurse from the clinic come by, talk to us plain: explain how it spreads, how it doesn’t. Knowledge helps. But so does sitting next to someone on a bench and realizing they’re tired from work, worried about rent, laughing at the same dumb squirrel stealing peas—just like you.

What makes people comfortable? Consistency. Kindness without expectation. Not pretending everything’s perfect—but showing up anyway. Tolerance isn’t about liking everything. It’s about deciding someone’s flaws or differences don’t cancel out their right to be here.

And yeah, we need more communication—especially when fear gets loud. Like when that rumor went around that asylum seekers were getting free housing while locals waited months. Turned out false, but it festered because nobody official came to clarify. Silence feeds suspicion.

We need town meetings where people can ask dumb questions without being shamed. Where the woman who’s scared of change can say so—and hear directly from the family who just crossed the border with nothing but a backpack and hope.

Because at the end of the day, most of us just want stability. A safe place. Someone who’ll notice if we’re gone.

So I believe in talking—even when it’s awkward. Even when I’m unsure. Because the garden only works if everyone tends their plot *and* watches the paths between them.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character18_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a hard one. I won’t pretend it isn’t.

When I was laid off after the clinic downsized—six months of nothing, applying everywhere, getting ghosted—I felt that fear deep in my bones. You start wondering if you’re invisible. And yeah, when I’d see job postings go to guys who just showed up with their duffel bags at 5 a.m., some from out of state, others from other countries, working cash under the table for less than minimum wage… it stung. It felt like the floor kept dropping.

But here’s what I also saw: those same guys rebuilding homes after the flood when no one else would do the dirty work. Working 12-hour shifts in 100-degree heat laying concrete, while locals complained the jobs “weren’t worth it” unless they paid benefits and overtime. And then turned them down.

Fairness, to me, ain’t about everyone getting the *same* job. It’s about having a *shot*. A real one. Not being shut out because you don’t know the right person, or you speak with an accent, or your papers aren’t perfect—or because you’ve got a record, or you’re on methadone, or people assume you’re lazy because you live in the projects.

I think we get too caught up in “us vs. them.” Like opportunity is a pie with only eight slices. But what if we’re not fighting over slices—but asking why the oven’s too small?

Most of the time, migrant workers aren’t taking jobs from locals—they’re doing jobs locals *won’t* do. The ones that break your back, pay pennies, offer no protection. They keep farms running, restaurants staffed, construction moving. Without them? Half the town would shut down.

But that doesn’t mean I don’t worry. When the packing plant hired all those new workers from Texas—some undocumented, some sent by temp agencies—and cut full-time positions to part-time with no benefits, that hit hard. My cousin lost his shift. He had two kids, a mortgage. That wasn’t fair.

So balance? It starts with rules that protect *everyone*. Because when employers can exploit one group, they end up lowering wages and conditions for *all* of us. I’ve seen it happen. An employer pays migrants under the table, no safety gear, no breaks—then turns around and says, “Can’t afford to raise wages for you locals either.”

That’s not competition. That’s cheating.

So if I had a say, I’d want policies that make sure *every* worker—born here or not—is paid fairly, treated safely, able to speak up without getting deported or fired. Union halls open to all. Labor boards that actually show up when someone complains. No more “just be grateful to have work” nonsense.

And for locals struggling? We need better training programs—real ones, not dead-end certificates. Childcare so parents can retrain. Transit so people can reach jobs outside the neighborhood. Stop acting like poverty is a moral failure.

Because the truth is, most of us—migrant or native-born—are playing the same rigged game. The divide-and-conquer thing? It works because we’re all scared. Scared of falling behind, scared of never catching up.

But if we stood together—locals and newcomers—demanding dignity, demanding a living wage, demanding housing and healthcare—that’d be powerful. I’ve seen it once or twice—at that strike at the warehouse last year. Black, white, Mexican, Haitian, even a few Appalachian boys like me—all standing in the rain with signs. Didn’t win everything. But we made ‘em listen.

So fairness? It’s not keeping people out. It’s making sure nobody gets thrown under the bus.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character18_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You know, I’ve sat in too many diner booths, heard too many versions of this argument. “They’re stealing our jobs.” “They’re bringing crime.” “At least they work hard.” People say all kinds of things—usually when they’re scared.

Let’s start with what I *know* from living here, not from headlines.

Immigrants fill jobs people aren’t doing. That’s not opinion—that’s fact. Who’s picking the strawberries at 5 a.m. in July? Who’s cleaning hotel rooms after midnight? Who’s working the night shift at the meatpacking plant where the air smells like blood and bleach? Not many folks from around here—not for that pay, not with those conditions. But the work gets done. And if it didn’t, shelves would empty. Restaurants would close. Farms would rot.

So yeah, labor shortage? Absolutely real in certain places, certain industries. I respect that argument. It’s practical. Keeps things running.

Cultural diversity—I’ll admit, I wasn’t always warm to it. Grew up in a town where everyone went to the same church, ate the same casseroles, celebrated the same holidays. Then I started working at the free clinic, and suddenly I’m taking vitals for a Guatemalan grandma who brings me tamales every Christmas “for good health,” or translating (badly) for a Syrian mom trying to explain her son’s asthma. And slowly, you realize—this ain’t an invasion. It’s life getting richer.

I never thought I’d crave injera instead of toast on Sunday mornings. Or learn how to wrap a scarf from Amina just so mine wouldn’t blow off in the wind. These little things—they don’t erase who I am. They add to it.

But then there’s the fear talk. Crime. Terrorism. Social tension.

Look—I get why people worry. You see a news story about some guy who crossed the border and later got arrested, and your stomach drops. Especially if you’ve been mugged before, or you live in a neighborhood that feels unstable. Fear feels personal.

But here’s what the numbers keep showing, even when we don’t want to hear it: immigrants commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born citizens. I didn’t believe it at first either. So I looked it up—CDC data, FBI stats, studies from universities. Over and over. It’s true. Even for undocumented folks. Doesn’t mean *every* one is a saint—but as a group? They’re not driving crime up.

Terrorism? That’s such a small piece, but it looms so big. One tragedy gets replayed for weeks. Meanwhile, domestic extremists—white supremacists, anti-government types—have caused more deaths on U.S. soil in the last twenty years, and we don’t call them a “threat to national identity.”

So why the double standard? Maybe because fear isn’t always about facts. It’s about *difference*. About not understanding someone’s language, their faith, their customs. When you don’t know someone, it’s easy to imagine the worst.

And yes—there *are* tensions. Newcomers move into a neighborhood, open a halal market, change the rhythm of the block, and some older residents feel pushed out. Like they’re losing their home. That pain is real. But the answer isn’t to shut the door. It’s to help people talk. To make space—for old and new both.

Humanitarian side? That hits me deep. I think about kids—refugees—coming alone, covered in dust, clutching a photo of a parent. Or women fleeing violence, showing scars under their sleeves. How can we turn away from that? My granddaddy fought in Korea, used to say America stood for something. Said we weren’t just a country—we were a promise.

I believe that. Or I want to.

But then comes the other fear—the quiet one people whisper about: *What if there’s not enough for us?* What if wages go down? What if housing gets tighter? Schools overcrowded?

That’s not just racism talking. That’s real anxiety when you’re barely making it yourself. When your kid’s classroom has 32 students and no aide, and you hear “more families are coming”—of course you panic.

But again, let’s look closer. Studies show mixed effects on wages—some small dip for low-skilled workers, maybe, in certain areas. But overall, immigrants also *create* jobs—open businesses, spend money, grow communities. Empty storefronts become bodegas, laundromats, repair shops. Tax dollars go up. Towns come back to life.

The problem isn’t immigration. It’s that we don’t invest enough in *everyone*. In schools. Infrastructure. healthcare. We pit people against each other instead of demanding better from the top.

So which views do I find reasonable?

- The labor argument: yes.
- Cultural vitality: yes, once you let it in.
- Humanitarian duty: absolutely—it’s who we should be.
- Concerns about strain on services: valid, but misdirected. Blame bad policy, not the people seeking help.
- Crime and terrorism fears: understandable emotionally, but not backed by evidence. Need more honest dialogue—and media responsibility.
- Wage fears: real for some, but oversimplified. The bigger issue is weak labor protections, not foreign birth.

We need to stop treating immigration like a crisis and start treating it like what it is—part of life. Like rain, or rent, or raising kids. Some days it’s hard. Some days it surprises you with beauty. Either way, we’re in it together.

And if we talked less about “them” and more about “us”—all of us trying to survive—maybe we’d find more common ground than we think.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character18_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for complete openness—that’s not realistic when schools are overcrowded, clinics understaffed, and folks here are already struggling to find decent housing. As much as my heart might want to say “let everyone in,” my gut knows we’d drown under the weight without support. And fairness means being honest about capacity.

But slamming the door? Refusing entry altogether? That’s cruel—and stupid. We need workers. We need people. Our population’s aging. Towns are emptying out. I’ve seen Main Street storefronts with weeds growing through the sidewalk. No one wins there.

So if I had to pick a mix—something that balances humanity, fairness, and reality—I’d go with **a combination of job-based admission *and* protected humanitarian pathways**, with **sensible numerical limits tied to regional needs**, not just national quotas that don’t reflect what’s actually happening on the ground.

Here’s how I see it:

We let people come based on real labor shortages—but with rules. Not just “fill the jobs,” but make sure those jobs pay fairly, have safety standards, and can’t be used to undercut local wages. Employers shouldn’t get a cheap workforce pass because someone’s scared to complain. If you’re hiring migrant workers, you follow the same laws as everyone else: minimum wage, overtime, OSHA compliance. No exceptions. Because when they suffer, we all suffer.

And—not either/or—we keep strong refugee and asylum protections. Period. If someone’s fleeing violence, persecution, war—if they’ve got proof, if they’ve gone through screening—then we take them in. Not because we’re saints, but because it’s right. And honestly? Refugees work hard. I’ve seen it. They rebuild their lives from nothing. They open shops, pay taxes, raise families. They become part of the fabric.

But—and this is important—we need to pair that with **real integration support**. Not just “here’s a city, figure it out.” I’m talking language classes, help with housing, access to healthcare, school enrollment for kids. Not handouts—just a fair start. And communities should get federal aid when they take in new arrivals, so locals don’t feel like they’re losing out. Help the schools hire more staff. Expand the clinic hours. Fix the roads.

Set numbers—yes—but make them flexible. Let regions apply for more slots if farms need seasonal workers or factories can’t fill shifts. And rotate so it’s not always the same towns bearing the load. Spread it out. Share the responsibility.

And while we’re at it? Fix the backlog. People waiting ten, fifteen years to legalize their status—some of them been here since I was in high school—working, paying rent, raising American-born kids. That’s not a system. That’s cruelty disguised as law.

A balanced policy, to me, protects workers—*all* workers—welcomes people in need, respects community limits, and invests in making integration work. It says: “We have room—but we need order. We care—but we also need stability.”

And above all? It stops treating immigration like an emergency every single year. This isn’t a flood. It’s a constant flow—like water in a river. We build better banks. We reinforce the bridges. We don’t just scream and run every time it rains.

Fairness means no free passes—but no scapegoats either. Integration means we all adjust. Not just newcomers learning English, but locals learning to sit beside someone different and still see a neighbor.

That’s the kind of country I believe in. Not perfect. But trying.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character18_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character18_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly… yeah. I did learn something.

When you first asked me to do this—to really step into her words, her thoughts—I thought I knew what she’d say. I was close to her. I remember our talks, the fire in her voice when injustice came up, how she’d tap her fingers when thinking, like she was typing out truth on an invisible keyboard. But speaking *as* her today—going deeper than memory—brought her back in a way I didn’t expect.

I realized something: she wasn’t just compassionate because it felt right. She was compassionate because she’d *seen* the cost of hardness. She saw her uncle lose everything after his DUI, watched people turn away from him like he was garbage. She saw how fast someone can go from “one of us” to “nobody’s problem.” And that shaped her—not as pity, but as principle.

And that changed how I think about my own views.

I’ll admit, before today, I’ve sometimes leaned harder on the practical side—wages, jobs, resources—like those were separate from the human part. Like we had to choose: head or heart.

But channeling her reminded me they’re not separate. Her fairness wasn’t soft—it was stubborn. It said: *You don’t get to claim community only when it’s convenient.* You don’t get to shut the door after you came through it.

She didn’t ignore fear—hers or others’. She named it. Felt it. But then she asked, *“What are we doing with that fear? Are we building walls—or bridges?”*

And that question? It landed differently today.

Because I see now that when I worry about jobs, or strain on schools, I’m not wrong to feel that. But if I stop there—if I let that fear harden into blame—I become part of the problem. Just like the bosses who play workers against each other to keep wages low.

Character18_F wouldn’t have wanted us divided—local vs. migrant, poor vs. poorer. She’d want us asking better questions: *Why isn’t there enough? Why are we fighting for scraps instead of demanding more?*

So yeah, this changed me.

Not that I have all the answers. But I feel clearer about the direction. Toward dignity. Toward inclusion that doesn’t pretend everything’s easy—but insists we figure it out *together*.

And hearing her voice again—even through me—it made me miss her less… and miss what she stood for more.

Because she wasn’t special for having these views. She was special for *living* them. In the garden. At the clinic. At the potluck. In the hard conversations with family.

That’s the legacy. Not just remembering her. But continuing her work—in how we treat the person next to us, especially when they’re different, especially when it’s hard.

And if that’s immigration policy… then maybe policy starts much smaller.  
With a chair pulled out.  
A thermos shared.  
A name learned, pronounced right.  

That’s where belonging begins.
